To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
VMH lesions or ventral noradrenaline depletion cause hyperphagia, increased feeding reward, and obesity.

medial hypothalamic and ventral midbrain damage increase food intake and LH self-stimulation; that contralateral far lateral hypothalamic damage decreases both; and that these findings are consistent with the hypothesis that LH self-stimulation is a measure of feeding reward.
the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus is necessary to prevent excessive feeding, and that the ventral norade-nergic bundle is also necessary to prevent excessive eating.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms that regulate feeding and feeding reward.
how the medial and lateral hypothalamus interact to regulate feeding.
the neurochemical basis of food intake and self-stimulation, which may have important implications for the understanding and control of obesity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LH region, including the VMH and ventral midbrain, plays a major role in the control of feeding and the reward value of food.
the VMH, the far-LH, and the ventral midbrain are all involved in the control of both feeding and feeding reward, and that the three areas interact in the control of these functions.
the LH is a major site of integration of the neural systems that regulate feeding and feeding reward.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the VMH inhibits feeding and feeding reward and that the far-LH inhibits feeding reward but not food intake.

the medial hypothalamus is critical for the normal inhibition of feeding, that the lateral hypothalamus is necessary for normal feeding and feeding reward, and that the VNAB is critical for the inhibition of feeding and self-stimation.
the VMH is necessary for the inhibition of feeding and that the LH is necessary for the reward properties of food intake.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LH is a critical site for the control of feeding and self-stimulating behavior.
the medial hypothalamus is necessary to inhibit both feeding and feeding reward, whereas the lateral hypothalamus is involved in the positive reinforcement of feeding.
the VMH is necessary for normal control of feeding and feeding-related reward, and that catecholamine neurons in the ventral midbrain can modulate both feeding and self-stimulated eating.
